lines.content: **ByLine** is a desktop contact manager for journalists. It helps journalists identify relevant contacts and keep track of interviewees for their reporting work.

Journalists work with a large and constantly growing network of sources, experts and interviewees, often across several stories at once. These contacts usually end up scattered across notebooks, message threads and phone records, making it hard to find the right person when a story breaks.

ByLine brings all of these contacts into one place. Journalists can record each contact's details, categorise them with tags (for example by expertise), and quickly search through their contact list to find people they might need. ByLine is optimised for users who type fast and prefer typing over other means of input.
ByLine is designed for **journalists who manage numerous professional contacts** with varying relationship strengths and areas of expertise, and who:
* juggle multiple stories at the same time
* need to quickly find the right source or interviewee for a story
* prefer typing commands over clicking through menus

**Example user:** Kimberly is an experienced journalist working on several stories at once. Her contacts are spread across scattered notes, messages and phone records, and she needs a single place to organise them and find the right person quickly.
* **Add a contact**: Record a contact's name, phone number, email and address, with optional tags.
e.g. `add n/Jane Tan p/91234567 e/jane@example.com a/12 Kent Ridge Road t/economist`
* **Edit a contact**: Change any of a contact's details, using the ID shown on its card.
* **Delete a contact**: Remove a contact using the ID shown on its card.
* **List contacts**: Show your active contacts, only archived contacts, or every contact.
* **Tag and untag contacts**: Add or remove tags without retyping the contact's other tags.
* **Search contacts**: Find contacts using part of a contact’s name, phone number, email, address or tags.
e.g. `find n/Tan t/econ` finds contacts with `Tan` in their name and a tag containing `econ`, such as `economics`
* **Filter contacts by tag**: Show only contacts that have every tag you name. Tags must match in full.
* **Sort contacts**: Order the contacts shown by name, phone, email, address or tag.
* **Archive and restore contacts**: Hide contacts you are no longer working with, without deleting them, and bring them back later.
* **Undo and redo**: Reverse your last change, or redo a change you undid.
* **Back up and load contacts**: Save all your contacts to a file and load them back later.

See the [User Guide](https://ay2627s1-cs2103-f13-1.github.io/tp/UserGuide.html) for every command, and the [Developer Guide](https://ay2627s1-cs2103-f13-1.github.io/tp/DeveloperGuide.html) for how ByLine is built.
This project is based on the AddressBook-Level3 project created by the [SE-EDU initiative](https://se-education.org).

Team members used AI tools, including ChatGPT Codex and Claude Code, throughout the project: to write and change code, to generate tests (for example, all the test classes for the Find feature), and to draft and edit documentation such as this guide and the User Guide. * `Search#levenshteinDistance` was generated with ChatGPT Codex, based on the `levenshtein_distance_vec` implementation in [tkarabela's fuzzy text search notebook](https://github.com/tkarabela/bigpython/blob/master/003--fuzzy-text-search/fuzzy-text-search.ipynb), and adapted to Java with two-row storage and optional substring matching. The following provides a quick overview of the main components and their interactions.

**`Main`** (consisting of classes [`Main`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103-F13-1/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/Main.java) and [`MainApp`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103-F13-1/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/MainApp.java)) is in charge of the app launch and shut down.
* At app launch, it initializes the other components in the correct sequence, and connects them up with each other.
* At shut down, it shuts down the other components and invokes cleanup methods where necessary.
The bulk of the app's work is done by the following four components:
* [**`Model`**](#model-component): Holds the data of the App in memory.
* [**`Storage`**](#storage-component): Reads data from, and writes data to, the hard disk.
[**`Commons`**](#common-classes) represents a collection of classes used by multiple other components.

This section describes some noteworthy details on how certain features are implemented.

Every contact has a `PersonId`, a whole number from 1 to `PersonId.MAX_VALUE` (999999). Commands that act on one contact, such as `edit`, `delete`, `tag`, `untag`, `archive` and `restore`, select the contact by this ID instead of by its position in the displayed list.

`AddressBook` holds a counter, `nextPersonId`, starting at 1. When `AddressBook#addPerson(Person)` receives a person without an ID, it gives the person the ID `nextPersonId` and moves the counter on. A person that already has an ID keeps it, and the counter moves past that ID if needed, so a new ID is always higher than every ID in use.
The counter only moves forward. Deleting a person does not lower it, and `clear` creates the new, empty address book with the same counter, so a deleted ID is never given out again.

`EditCommand`, `TagCommand`, `UntagCommand`, `ArchiveCommand` and `RestoreCommand` replace a person with an updated copy. Each copy keeps the original's ID, and `AddressBook#setPerson` rejects a copy whose ID differs.

Once ID 999999 has been given out, the counter is 1000000 and `AddressBook#hasAvailablePersonId()` returns false. `AddCommand` checks `Model#hasAvailablePersonId()` and shows an error instead of adding the person. Because the largest ID is far below the largest `int`, the counter can never overflow and wrap around to an ID in use.

1. The command's parser calls `ParserUtil#parsePersonId` on the preamble, which contains the number before the first prefix, e.g. the `3` in `edit 3 p/91234567`. Anything that is not a whole number from 1 to 999999 gives the invalid command format message.
2. The parser creates the command with the parsed `PersonId`, stored as `targetId`.

3. When the command runs, it calls `Model#findPersonById(targetId)`, which searches the **whole** address book, not only the displayed list. A contact hidden by `find`, moved by `sort` or archived can therefore still be selected. The command unwraps the returned `Optional<Person>`. If no contact has the ID, it throws a `CommandException` with `No contact has the ID 3.`

New commands that act on one contact should parse a `PersonId` with `ParserUtil#parsePersonId` and wrap parsing failures in the command's invalid-format usage message. Each command looks up the ID during execution and converts an empty result into a `CommandException` using `Messages.MESSAGE_PERSON_ID_NOT_FOUND`.
`JsonAdaptedPerson` saves each ID as text, e.g. `"id" : "3"`, and `JsonSerializableAddressBook` saves the counter as `"nextPersonId"`. When the file is loaded:
* The counter is raised above the highest saved ID if needed, so a hand-edited counter cannot cause an ID to be reused.
* The file is rejected as invalid if two persons have the same ID, an ID is outside 1 to 999999, or `nextPersonId` is outside 1 to 1000000.
* Persons saved without an ID (data from before IDs were added) are given new IDs, and `JsonAddressBookStorage` saves the file again straight away so that those IDs are kept.

* Pros: The same number always means the same contact, whatever is displayed. A contact hidden by `find` or moved by `sort` can still be edited or deleted, and there is no risk of acting on the wrong contact after the list changes.
* Cons: Users read the ID from the card instead of counting positions, and IDs must be saved and kept unique.
* **Alternative 2: The position in the displayed list (AB3's original design).**
* Pros: Nothing extra needs to be stored.
* Cons: The same number points to a different contact after `find`, `sort` or a deletion, so it is easy to edit or delete the wrong contact.
* Pros: An ID that a journalist has noted down never points to a different contact later.
* Cons: IDs have gaps, and the limit of 999999 applies to every contact ever added, not just the ones currently stored.
* Pros: IDs stay small and have no gaps.
* Cons: An old ID can suddenly mean a different contact, which is the problem persistent IDs are meant to solve.

`TagCommandParser` and `UntagCommandParser` read the contact's ID with `ParserUtil#parsePersonId` (see [Contact ID feature](#contact-id-feature)) and the tags with `ParserUtil#parseTags`. At least one `t/` prefix is required. Otherwise, the parser throws a `ParseException` with the command's usage message.

When executed, both commands find the contact with `Model#findPersonById(targetId)`, then copy its tags into a new set. `TagCommand` adds the given tags to the set, and `UntagCommand` removes them. If the set does not change, because the contact already has every given tag (`tag`) or has none of them (`untag`), the command throws a `CommandException` and the contact is not changed. Otherwise, the command replaces the contact, through `Model#setPerson`, with a copy that has the new tags and the same ID, details and archive flag.

`Tag` saves its name in lowercase, and tags are compared by that name. A contact's tags are a `Set<Tag>`, so adding a tag the contact already has, in any upper/lower case, does not create a second copy, and removing a tag matches it regardless of case.
Unlike `edit t/…`, which replaces all of a contact's tags, `tag` and `untag` change only the tags given.
**Aspect: How tags are added and removed**
* Pros: A journalist can add or remove one tag without retyping the contact's other tags.
* Cons: Two more commands to learn.
* Cons: Changing one tag means retyping every other tag, and leaving one out removes it by mistake.
* Pros: `Expert` and `expert` are the same tag, so a contact cannot end up with both, and tags look consistent in the list.
* Cons: The capitalisation the journalist typed is lost.
* Pros: Tags look exactly as typed.
* Cons: Every comparison would need to ignore case separately, or near-identical tags would pile up.

`AddressBookParser` delegates `find` arguments to `FindCommandParser`. The parser tokenises all supported prefixes (`n/`, `p/`, `e/`, `a/` and `t/`) with `ArgumentTokenizer`, then passes the resulting `ArgumentMultimap` to a single `MatchPersonPredicate`.
The predicate combines the following conditions with AND. Matching is case-insensitive and uses consecutive substrings:

* **General substring:** `getPreamble()` returns the text before the first recognised prefix. A non-empty preamble must occur within the name, phone number, email, address or an individual tag. An empty preamble imposes no general restriction when prefixes are supplied.

* **Field substrings:** `getValue(...)` returns an `Optional<String>` for each of the name, phone, email and address prefixes. An absent prefix imposes no restriction. A present substring must occur within its corresponding field. If a prefix is repeated, `getValue(...)` returns its last value.

* **Tag substrings:** `getAllValues(PREFIX_TAG)` returns every supplied tag substring. Each must match at least one tag, but multiple substrings may match the same tag. An empty list imposes no tag restriction.
Part of the command | Read as | A contact matches if
`example` (before the first prefix) | general substring (preamble) | its name, phone, email, address or one of its tags contains `example`
`t/fri` | tag substring | at least one of its tags contains `fri`

The tokenizer trims surrounding whitespace from each value but keeps internal spaces, so the whole preamble is one substring even if it contains spaces. Text after a prefix belongs to that prefix until the next recognised prefix. For example, `find n/Alex example` has no preamble and searches names for `Alex example`.

Fuzzy matching is handled by `Search.substringThenLevenshtein(text, key)` for each general, field and tag comparison. It first checks for a case-insensitive substring match, then falls back to `levenshteinDistance` with partial matching enabled, comparing the entire key against any contiguous part of the field without penalising surrounding text. Insertions, deletions and substitutions each cost one edit, and spaces count as characters; the permitted distance is `floor(TOLERANCE * key.length())`, where `Search` owns the private constant `TOLERANCE = 1.0 / 4.0`. The calculation uses two rows of the distance table to limit memory use, and the predicate still requires every supplied search condition to match.

The parser does not reject empty input or duplicate prefixes. With no preamble or prefixes, the predicate returns false for every person. An empty name, phone, email or address substring matches every value of that field; an empty tag substring requires at least one tag.

`MatchPersonPredicate` implements `Predicate<Person>` and is passed to `FindCommand`. On execution, the command calls `Model.updateFilteredPersonList(predicate)` and reports the number of matching persons. The new predicate replaces the previous filter, so each search considers the whole address book. The predicate does not check the archive flag, so archived contacts appear in search results. The predicate is applied through the [displayed-list layers](#displayed-list-layers).
**Aspect: Matching the entire search text versus any whole-word keyword**
* **Alternative 1 (current choice): Match each search value as one consecutive substring.**

* Pros: Users can search using incomplete details, such as part of a name, phone number or email address. Spaces and word order remain meaningful: `Alex Yeoh` is treated as one search value instead of two alternatives, helping users narrow their search with a phrase.
* Cons: A phrase may miss a contact whose details contain the words in a different order or with additional text between them. Short substrings can still match unrelated contacts.
* **Alternative 2 (original behavior): Split the input into keywords and match any complete keyword.**
* Pros: A contact can match even if the user remembers only one correct word. Word order and intervening text do not matter, and users can search for several alternative names in one command.

* Cons: Adding keywords broadens the search instead of narrowing it. For example, `Alex Yeoh` also matches `Alex Tan` and `Bernice Yeoh`, which can make the intended contact harder to identify. Whole-word matching also prevents searching with partial words.

Matching the entire search value supports finding contacts from partial details while preserving the meaning of multi-word phrases. The current implementation also falls back to approximate substring matching through `Search.substringThenLevenshtein`, allowing limited typing errors at the cost of potentially including additional matches.
**Aspect: One combined predicate versus separate predicates for each search type**
* **Alternative 1 (current choice): Use one `MatchPersonPredicate` for general, field and combined searches.**

* Pros: `FindCommandParser` follows the same construction path for every supported combination of arguments. The predicate keeps the AND relationship between general, field and tag conditions in one place, so combined searches do not require separate parser branches.

* Cons: The predicate handles several kinds of conditions and depends on the parser's `ArgumentMultimap` representation. Adding search options can make it harder to read and increases the combinations that need testing.
* **Alternative 2: Use separate predicates for general and field-specific searches, composing them when needed.**
* Pros: Each predicate has a focused responsibility and can be tested or reused independently.

* Cons: The parser or a dedicated helper must select and compose the predicates for each combination of arguments. Shared matching rules may be duplicated unless they are extracted into common helpers.

A combined predicate keeps construction simple while supporting general and prefixed conditions in the same command. Separate predicates would become more useful if the search types developed substantially different rules or needed independent reuse.

`AddressBookParser` delegates `filter` arguments to `FilterCommandParser`. The parser tokenizes only `PREFIX_TAG`, rejects a non-empty preamble, requires at least one `t/` occurrence, and retrieves every tag value with `ArgumentMultimap#getAllValues(PREFIX_TAG)`. It passes the complete collection to `ParserUtil#parseTags`, so filter uses the same validation, trimming, lowercase normalisation, and error message as the rest of the application. The returned `Set<Tag>` also collapses repeated case-equivalent tags into one condition.

The parser constructs a `HasAllTagsPredicate` and wraps it in a `FilterCommand`. The predicate defensively copies the required tags and tests whether `Person#getTags()` contains all of them. Because `Tag#equals` compares the normalised complete tag name, matching is exact and case-insensitive. A separate predicate is used instead of `find`'s `MatchPersonPredicate` because find deliberately accepts partial tag substrings, whereas `filter` must not match `housing` against `housing policy`.

When executed, `FilterCommand` calls `Model#updateFilteredPersonList(predicate)` and reports the filtered size using `Messages#MESSAGE_PERSONS_LISTED_OVERVIEW`. Each filter evaluates the full stored address book instead of the currently displayed subset. The predicate does not inspect archive status, so matching archived contacts are included. See [Displayed-list layers](#displayed-list-layers) for how a new predicate replaces the displayed view and clears its previous sort.
If no contact matches, `FilterCommand` obtains every stored contact through `Model#getAddressBook()`, flattens their
tag sets, removes duplicate tag names, and sorts the remaining names alphabetically. The command appends this list to
its result as `Available tags: ...`; tags from archived contacts are included because filtering also includes archived
contacts. If the address book contains no tags, the command reports `Available tags: none`. This feedback does not
alter the exact-match predicate or any stored data.
Filtering changes only the displayed list; stored contact data never changes.
* **Alternative 1 (current choice): Match complete `Tag` values with a dedicated predicate.**
* Pros: `filter` has a clear purpose distinct from `find`, reuses `Tag` equality, and cannot accidentally match a broader tag.
* Cons: Users must type the complete tag value.
* Pros: Less new code and more forgiving input.
* Cons: `filter t/policy` would also match `housing policy` and `policy researcher`, duplicating `find` rather than providing exact grouping.
* **Alternative 1 (current choice): Require every specified tag (AND matching).**
* Pros: Adding a tag condition narrows results predictably and supports finding contacts who meet several reporting needs at once.
* Cons: Users may receive no results when no contact has the full combination.
* Pros: Produces a broader pool of contacts.
* Cons: Adding tags broadens rather than narrows the result and cannot directly express “has both tags”.

`AddressBookParser` delegates the arguments of a `sort` command to `SortCommandParser`. The parser validates the mandatory field and optional order, normalises both case-insensitively, defaults a missing order to ascending, and creates a `SortCommand`.

When executed, `SortCommand` selects a comparator through `PersonComparator` and asks the model to sort the displayed contacts. The model retains the stored contacts in `VersionedAddressBook`, exposes the selected subset through a `FilteredList`, and applies the comparator to a `SortedList` layered over that filtered view. This changes the order observed by the UI without reordering the stored address-book data.
The displayed-list layers are shown below.
`ModelManager#getFilteredPersonList()` returns the `SortedList`, so the UI always shows the filtered contacts in the current sort order.

Text fields are compared case-insensitively, phone numbers numerically, and tags by their alphabetically first tag. For tag sorting, contacts without tags remain after tagged contacts in both ascending and descending order. The comparator applies name-ascending tie-breaking. `ModelManager` then preserves the prior displayed order for contacts that remain completely tied. `list`, `find`, `filter`, `add` and `edit` call `updateFilteredPersonList`, which clears the `SortedList` comparator before replacing the predicate.
* **Alternative 1 (current choice): Use a sorted view of the filtered contacts.**
* Pros: Sorting affects exactly the contacts being displayed, composes with filtering, and cannot change the saved contact order.
* Cons: The model must maintain both `FilteredList` and `SortedList` view layers and explicitly clear the comparator when the display is replaced.
* **Alternative 2: Sort the stored contact list directly.**
* Pros: The UI could display the reordered storage list without another view layer.

* Cons: A display-only command would mutate persistent ordering, filtering would be harder to isolate, and the changed order could be saved unintentionally. This alternative was rejected because sorting is specified as a temporary presentation operation.

Each `Person` has an `archived` flag, which is `false` for new contacts. `ArchiveCommand` and `RestoreCommand` select the contact by calling `Model#findPersonById(targetId)` and unwrapping the result (see [Contact ID feature](#contact-id-feature)), then replace it with a copy whose flag is `true` or `false`. All other fields, including the ID, are copied unchanged. Archiving a contact that is already archived, or restoring one that is not, throws a `CommandException` and changes nothing.

`JsonAdaptedPerson` saves the flag as `"archived"`. Files saved before archiving existed have no such field, so their contacts load as not archived. `PersonCard` adds `[Archived]` after the name of an archived contact.

`ListCommandParser` turns `list`, `list all` and `list archive` into a `ListCommand` with the view `ACTIVE`, `ALL` or `ARCHIVED`. The keyword is trimmed and compared case-insensitively, and any other input throws a `ParseException` with `ListCommand.MESSAGE_USAGE`. Each view calls `Model#updateFilteredPersonList` with `PREDICATE_SHOW_ACTIVE_PERSONS`, `PREDICATE_SHOW_ALL_PERSONS` or `PREDICATE_SHOW_ARCHIVED_PERSONS`. These predicates are applied through the [displayed-list layers](#displayed-list-layers).

`ModelManager` starts with `PREDICATE_SHOW_ACTIVE_PERSONS`, so archived contacts are hidden when ByLine starts. `Model#addPerson` switches back to this predicate, since a new contact is never archived. `EditCommand` switches to `PREDICATE_SHOW_ARCHIVED_PERSONS` if the edited contact is archived and to `PREDICATE_SHOW_ACTIVE_PERSONS` otherwise, so the edited contact stays displayed.

Other commands, such as `find`, `tag` and `delete`, treat archived contacts like any other contact. `EditCommand`, `TagCommand` and `UntagCommand` copy the flag into the updated person, so changing a contact's details does not restore it.
* **Alternative 1 (current choice): A flag on each `Person`, in the same list as other contacts.**
* Pros: An archived contact keeps its ID and details, and every command that selects a contact by ID works on it unchanged.
* Cons: Every command that creates an updated `Person` must remember to copy the flag.
* **Alternative 2: A separate list of archived contacts.**
* Pros: Active and archived contacts are clearly separated.
* Cons: Looking up an ID would have to search two lists, and archiving would move a contact between lists.

`AddressBookParser` passes the arguments of `export` and `load` to `BackupCommandParser`, which reads the whole argument as a file path. Surrounding double quotes are removed, and a blank path gives the command's usage message. For `load`, `.json` is added if the path does not end with it. For `export`, the file is always saved as JSON: a missing extension gets `.json`, and any other final extension is replaced, so `backup.csv` becomes `backup.json`.

`ExportCommand` calls `BackupStorage#exportAddressBook`, which writes every contact, including archived contacts, and the ID counter to the file in the same JSON format as the main data file. The file is created with `CREATE_NEW`, so it never replaces an existing file by itself. `LogicManager` returns straight after `export`, without calling `Model#commitAddressBook()` or saving the main data file, because the address book has not changed.
If the file already exists, `LogicManager` asks the journalist to confirm instead of showing an error:
1. It catches the `CommandException` caused by the existing file, stores the destination in `pendingExportPath`, and shows a warning ending with `Proceed? (Y/N)`.

2. While `pendingExportPath` is set, `LogicManager#execute` treats the next input as the answer instead of parsing it as a command. `N`, in either case, cancels and leaves the file unchanged. Any input other than `Y` or `N` repeats the warning.

3. `Y` calls `BackupStorage#overwriteAddressBook`, which writes the contacts to a temporary file in the same folder and then moves it over the old file, so the old backup is kept if writing fails. As with a normal export, nothing is committed or saved to the main data file.

2. `LogicManager` saves the current contacts to a new `before-load-<timestamp>-<random id>.json` file in the same folder as the backup, using `BackupStorage#backupBeforeLoad`. This is skipped if the address book is empty or equals the sample data. If the copy cannot be saved, the load is cancelled.

The undo/redo mechanism is facilitated by `VersionedAddressBook`. It extends `AddressBook` with an undo/redo history, stored internally as `states`, a list of `AddressBook` copies, and `currentStateIndex`. It implements the following operations:
* `VersionedAddressBook#commit()` — Saves the current address book state in its history, unless it is the same as the current saved state.
* `VersionedAddressBook#undo()` — Restores the previous address book state from its history.
* `VersionedAddressBook#redo()` — Restores a previously undone address book state from its history.

These operations are exposed in the `Model` interface as `Model#commitAddressBook()`, `Model#undoAddressBook()` and `Model#redoAddressBook()` respectively, along with `Model#canUndoAddressBook()` and `Model#canRedoAddressBook()`.

`LogicManager#execute` calls `Model#commitAddressBook()` after every command that executes successfully, except `export`, which changes no data. For `load`, this happens only after the backup copy and the data file are saved (see [Export and load feature](#export-and-load-feature)). Individual commands never call it. Because `commit()` ignores a state equal to the current saved state, only commands that changed the address book add a state. New commands that change data are therefore undoable without any extra code.

Each saved state is a copy made with `new AddressBook(...)`, which includes the ID counter `nextPersonId`. Undoing an `add` therefore also rolls the counter back, so the next contact added gets the undone contact's ID. The history keeps the initial state plus at most `VersionedAddressBook.HISTORY_LIMIT` (20) changes. When a commit would exceed this, the oldest state is removed.
Given below is an example usage scenario and how the undo/redo mechanism behaves at each step.
Step 1. The user launches the application. The `VersionedAddressBook` will be initialized with the initial address book state, and `currentStateIndex` pointing to that single address book state.

Step 2. The user executes `delete 5` command to delete the contact with ID 5. After the command runs, `LogicManager` calls `Model#commitAddressBook()`. The address book has changed, so its new state is saved in `states`, and `currentStateIndex` is shifted to the newly inserted address book state.
Step 3. The user executes `add n/David …​` to add a new person. `LogicManager` again calls `Model#commitAddressBook()`, causing another modified address book state to be saved into `states`.

<div markdown="span" class="alert alert-info">:information_source: **Note:** If a command fails, it throws an exception before `LogicManager` reaches `Model#commitAddressBook()`, so no state is saved.

Step 4. The user now decides that adding the person was a mistake, and decides to undo that action by executing the `undo` command. The `undo` command will call `Model#undoAddressBook()`, which will shift `currentStateIndex` once to the left, pointing it to the previous address book state, and restores the address book to that state.

<div markdown="span" class="alert alert-info">:information_source: **Note:** If `currentStateIndex` is 0, pointing to the initial address book state, then there are no previous address book states to restore. The `undo` command uses `Model#canUndoAddressBook()` to check if this is the case. If so, it shows `There is nothing to undo.` rather than attempting to perform the undo.

The `redo` command does the opposite — it calls `Model#redoAddressBook()`, which shifts `currentStateIndex` once to the right, pointing to the previously undone state, and restores the address book to that state.

<div markdown="span" class="alert alert-info">:information_source: **Note:** If `currentStateIndex` is at index `states.size() - 1`, pointing to the latest address book state, then there are no undone address book states to restore. The `redo` command uses `Model#canRedoAddressBook()` to check if this is the case. If so, it shows `There is nothing to redo.` rather than attempting to perform the redo.

Step 5. The user then decides to execute the command `list`. `LogicManager` still calls `Model#commitAddressBook()` after `list`, but the address book equals the current saved state, so `commit()` saves nothing. The same happens after `undo` and `redo`, since the address book then equals the state just restored. Thus, `states` remains unchanged.

Step 6. The user executes `clear`. When `LogicManager` calls `Model#commitAddressBook()` after `clear`, the address book has changed and `currentStateIndex` is not at the end of `states`, so all states after it are purged before the new state is saved. Reason: It no longer makes sense to redo the `add n/David …​` command. This is the behavior that most modern desktop applications follow.

* **Alternative 1 (current choice):** Saves the entire address book.
* Pros: Easy to implement. Saved states share the same immutable `Person` objects, so each state costs only a list of references.
* Cons: May have performance issues in terms of memory usage.

* Pros: Will use less memory (e.g. for `delete`, just save the person being deleted).

* **Alternative 1 (current choice):** `LogicManager` calls `Model#commitAddressBook()` after every successful command, and `VersionedAddressBook#commit()` skips states that equal the current one.
* Pros: Commands need no undo-related code, and new commands that change data are undoable automatically.
* Cons: Every command costs one comparison of the whole address book, even if it changed nothing.
* **Alternative 2:** Each command that changes data calls `Model#commitAddressBook()` itself.
* Pros: Commands that do not change data cost nothing extra.
* Cons: Every new command that changes data must remember the call, or it silently cannot be undone.
**Aspect: What happens to the ID counter on undo**
* **Alternative 1 (current choice):** The counter is part of each saved state, so undo rolls it back.
* Pros: Undo restores the address book exactly as it was, and an undone `add` leaves no gap in the IDs.
* Cons: The ID of an undone contact is given to the next contact added, so IDs are not strictly never reused.
* **Alternative 2:** The counter is never rolled back.
* Pros: IDs are never reused, even after undo.
* Cons: The restored state differs from the saved one, and undone additions leave gaps in the IDs.

These requirements define the quality targets and operating constraints for ByLine.
1. **Keyboard usability:** After launch, journalists should be able to add, list, edit, delete, tag,
search, and filter contacts using only the keyboard.
2. **Typing efficiency:** A journalist who types at 40 words per minute should be able to add a contact with a name,
phone number, email and address in under 30 seconds.
3. **Capacity and performance:** ByLine should support 1,000 contacts. With that dataset, adding,
listing, editing, deleting, tagging, searching, and filtering contacts should each display a result within
one second on a machine with at least a dual-core 2 GHz processor, 8 GB RAM, local SSD storage,
and Java 25, with no other resource-intensive applications running. This target applies to

4. **Platform compatibility:** ByLine should run as a desktop application on Windows, macOS,

5. **Offline operation:** After installation, managing contacts and saving or loading contact data

6. **Local storage format:** Contact data should be stored in a human-readable JSON file on the journalist's
computer, so that it can be copied or backed up without ByLine.

8. **Screen sizes:** The GUI should work well, with no content cut off, on screens of 1920x1080 or higher at 100%

* **AB3**: AddressBook Level 3, the application on which ByLine is based. Some inherited class names and implementation details continue to use AB3 terminology.
* **Active contact**: A contact that is not archived. `list` shows only active contacts.
* **Address book**: The internal collection that stores all contact records. This name is inherited from AB3 and is represented by the `AddressBook` class in the codebase.
* **Archived contact**: A contact hidden with `archive`. It keeps its ID and details, is not shown by `list`, and can be brought back with `restore`.
* **Backup file**: A JSON file holding a copy of all contacts, which `load` can read. `export` creates one, and `load` also creates one (named `before-load-…`) before replacing the contacts.

* **ByLine**: A desktop, CLI-based contact-management application that helps journalists organise and retrieve professional contacts relevant to their reporting. Users interact with ByLine primarily by typing commands, while a GUI displays their contacts and command results.
* **Case-insensitive matching**: Comparing text without treating uppercase and lowercase letters as different. For example, `Housing` and `housing` are considered equivalent.
* **CLI (Command Line Interface)**: A text-based interface through which users operate ByLine by typing commands.
* **Command**: A text instruction entered through the CLI to perform an operation, such as adding, listing, deleting, tagging, or searching for contacts.
* **Command Guide**: The list of commands, with their formats and examples, that `help` shows in the panel on the right.
* **Command prefix**: A marker that identifies the meaning of a command parameter, such as `n/` for a name or `t/` for a tag.
* **Complete contact list**: All contacts stored in ByLine, regardless of the contacts currently displayed in the UI.
* **Contact**: A person whose details a journalist stores in ByLine because the person may be relevant to current or future reporting.
* **Contact details panel**: The panel on the right that shows all of the selected contact's details, including whether it is archived.

* **Contact ID**: The number shown as `ID: 3` on a contact's card. A contact gets the next unused ID when it is added and keeps it permanently. IDs are never reused. Commands that act on one contact select it by this ID.
* **Contact record**: The complete set of information stored about one contact, including their name, phone number, email address, address, and tags.
* **Displayed contact list**: The contacts currently shown. `list`, `find` and `filter` choose which contacts are shown, and `sort` sets their order.
* **Duplicate contact**: A contact whose name and phone number match an existing contact's. Names are compared after
letter case is ignored and each run of spaces is treated as one space. ByLine does not allow duplicate contacts.
* **Duplicate tag**: A tag that is already assigned to a contact or is repeated within the same command, ignoring letter case.
* **Exact tag match**: A match in which the requested tag equals a complete stored tag value, ignoring letter case. A requested tag `policy` does not exactly match `housing policy`.
* **Expert**: A contact with specialist knowledge relevant to a story or topic.
* **Fuzzy matching**: Matching that allows small typing mistakes. `find` allows about one wrong, missing or extra character for every four characters typed.
* **GUI (Graphical User Interface)**: The visual interface that displays the command box, contact list, command results, and other application information.
* **Interviewee**: A contact whom a journalist has interviewed or intends to interview.
* **Journalist**: The target user of ByLine, who manages professional contacts for reporting purposes and prefers a command-driven desktop application.
* **MSS (Main Success Scenario)**: The steps of a use case when nothing goes wrong.
* **Partial match**: A match that occurs when a search value appears within a stored field without being equal to the complete field value.

* **Person**: The internal model entity used to represent a contact. This term is inherited from AB3 and appears in class names such as `Person` and `UniquePersonList`; user-facing documentation should use **contact** instead.
* **Preamble**: The text between the command word and the first prefix, e.g. `example` in `find example n/Alex`, or `3` in `edit 3 p/91234567`.
* **Search criterion**: A field and value used to restrict search results, such as a name, phone number, email address, address, or tag.
* **Source**: A contact who provides, or may provide, information, evidence, background, or commentary for a journalist's reporting.
* **Story**: A news article, investigation, or other reporting assignment on which a journalist is working.
* **Tag**: A journalist-defined label assigned to a contact to represent an area of expertise, topic, role, organisation, or another useful characteristic.
* **Topic**: A subject area used to describe the focus of a story or a contact's relevance, such as housing policy or public health.

ByLine is a **desktop contact manager for journalists**. It helps you keep track of sources, experts and interviewees, tag them by topic, and find the right person quickly when a story breaks. You use ByLine by typing commands (a Command Line Interface, or CLI), and the window shows your contacts and the results. If you type quickly, this is faster than clicking through menus.
1. Ensure that Java `25` or later is installed on your computer.
**Mac users:** Ensure you have the precise JDK version prescribed [here](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/javaInstallationMac.html).
3. Copy the file to the folder you want to use as the _home folder_ for your ByLine.
4. Open a terminal, `cd` to the folder containing the JAR file, and run `java -jar ByLine.jar`.
A GUI similar to the one below should appear in a few seconds. Note how the app contains some sample data.
5. Type a command in the command box and press Enter to execute it. For example, type **`help`** and press Enter to show the command guide.
Some example commands you can try:
* `add n/John Doe p/98765432 e/johnd@example.com a/John street, block 123, #01-01` : Adds a contact named `John Doe` to ByLine.
* `delete 3` : Deletes the contact with ID 3. Each contact's ID is shown as `ID: 3` on its card.
6. Refer to the [Features](#features) section below for details of each command.
* Words in `UPPER_CASE` are the parameters to be supplied by the user.
For example, in `add n/NAME`, replace `NAME` with a value such as `John Doe`.
* A prefix, such as `n/` or `t/`, tells ByLine which detail comes next.
For example, in `add n/John Doe p/98765432`, the name follows `n/` and the phone number follows `p/`.
* Items in square brackets are optional.
For example, `n/NAME [t/TAG]` can be used as `n/John Doe t/friend` or as `n/John Doe`.
* Items followed by `…`​ can appear zero or more times.
For example, `[t/TAG]…​` may be omitted, or written as `t/friend` or `t/friend t/family`.
* Parameters can be in any order.
For example, if the command specifies `n/NAME p/PHONE_NUMBER`, `p/PHONE_NUMBER n/NAME` is also acceptable.
* Extraneous parameters for commands that take no parameters, such as `help`, `exit`, and `clear`, are ignored.
For example, `help 123` is interpreted as `help`. The exceptions are `undo` and `redo`, which show an error instead, so that `undo 3` is not mistaken for undoing three changes.

* If you are using a PDF version of this document, be careful when copying and pasting commands that span multiple lines as space characters surrounding line-breaks may be omitted when copied over to the application.
Every contact has an ID, a whole number shown as `ID: 3` on the contact's card. Commands that act on one contact, such as `edit` and `delete`, use this ID to pick the contact.
* A new contact gets the next unused ID. The first contact is `1`, the next is `2`, and so on.
* A contact keeps its ID for good. The ID does not change when you use `find`, `filter`, `sort` or `list`, archive the contact, or restart ByLine.
* Commands find the contact by its ID even if it is not in the list currently shown, e.g. after a `find`.

* IDs are never reused. After you delete a contact or run `clear`, the next new contact still gets a new ID. The one exception is [undoing](#undoing-a-change-undo) an `add`, which frees that contact's ID for the next contact you add.
* Type the ID as a plain number, e.g. `delete 3`.
* IDs go up to 999999. Because IDs are never reused, no more contacts can be added once ID 999999 has been given out.
Name `n/` | English letters (A–Z), numbers and spaces. Must not start with a space.
Phone `p/` | Digits only, at least 3 digits.
Address `a/` | Any text, but not blank.
Tag `t/` | Letters in any language, numbers and spaces, e.g. `housing policy`. Saved in lowercase.

Two contacts can't have the same name **and** phone number. ByLine ignores upper/lower case and extra spaces when comparing names, so `John Doe` and `john doe` with the same phone number count as the same contact. Contacts with the same name but different phone numbers are allowed. Names are saved exactly as you typed them.

Edits an existing contact in ByLine.
* Edits the contact with the given `ID`, shown as `ID: 3` on the contact's card. See [Contact IDs](#contact-ids).
* If no contact has that ID, ByLine shows `No contact has the ID 3.` and nothing is changed.
* At least one of the optional fields must be provided.
* Existing values will be updated to the input values.
* If the new name and phone number match another contact's, ByLine rejects the edit. See [Contact details](#contact-details).
* When editing tags, all of the contact's existing tags are removed; adding tags is not cumulative.
* To remove all of a contact's tags, enter `t/` without a tag after it.
* To add or remove only some tags, use [`tag`](#adding-tags-to-a-contact-tag) or [`untag`](#removing-tags-from-a-contact-untag) instead.
* After the edit, ByLine shows the group the contact is in: your active contacts, or your archived contacts if the edited contact is archived. The edited contact stays in view.
*  `edit 1 p/91234567 e/johndoe@example.com` Edits the phone number and email address of the contact with ID 1 to be `91234567` and `johndoe@example.com` respectively.
*  `edit 2 n/Betsy Crower t/` Edits the name of the contact with ID 2 to be `Betsy Crower` and clears all existing tags.
Deletes the specified contact from ByLine.
* Deletes the contact with the given `ID`, shown as `ID: 3` on the contact's card. See [Contact IDs](#contact-ids).
* The contact is deleted even if it is not in the list currently shown.
* If no contact has that ID, ByLine shows `No contact has the ID 3.` and nothing is deleted.
* The deleted contact's ID is never given to another contact.
* `find Betsy` shows the matching contacts with their IDs. If Betsy's card shows `ID: 5`, `delete 5` deletes that contact.
Adds one or more tags to a contact, keeping the tags it already has.
* Adds the given tags to the contact with the given `ID`. See [Contact IDs](#contact-ids).
* At least one tag must be given.
* See [Contact details](#contact-details) for what a tag can contain.
* Tags are saved in lowercase, so `t/Expert` is saved as `expert`. Tags that differ only in upper/lower case count as the same tag.
* If the contact already has every given tag, ByLine shows `No tags were added because the contact already has the specified tags.`
* `tag 3 t/expert` adds the tag `expert` to the contact with ID 3.
* `tag 3 t/housing policy t/interviewee` adds the tags `housing policy` and `interviewee` to the contact with ID 3.
Removes one or more tags from a contact, keeping its other tags.
* Removes the given tags from the contact with the given `ID`. See [Contact IDs](#contact-ids).
* At least one tag must be given.
* Tags are matched ignoring upper/lower case, so `t/Expert` removes the tag `expert`.
* If the contact has none of the given tags, ByLine shows `No tags were removed because the contact does not have the specified tags.`
* `untag 3 t/expert` removes the tag `expert` from the contact with ID 3.
* `untag 3 t/housing policy t/interviewee` removes both tags from the contact with ID 3.
* `list` shows only active contacts, i.e. contacts that are not archived. ByLine also shows these when it starts.
* `list all` shows all contacts, including archived ones.
* `all` and `archive` can be typed in upper or lower case, e.g. `list ARCHIVE`.
* Any other input, such as `list archived`, shows an error listing the accepted formats, and the displayed list stays the same.
Finds contacts using part of their details, such as part of a name or phone number.
* `TEXT`, typed without a prefix, is searched for in every detail: name, phone number, email, address and tags. Put it before any prefix.
* Text after a prefix is searched for only in that detail. For example, `n/Al` searches names only.
* A contact is shown only if it matches **everything** you give, so adding more conditions narrows the results.
* Upper/lower case does not matter: `al` matches both `Alex` and `Balakrishnan`.
* The text you type is matched as a whole, including spaces: `Alex Ye` matches `Alex Yeoh`, but `Ye Alex` does not.

* Small typing mistakes are allowed: about one wrong, missing or extra character for every four characters you type. For example, `find n/Bernise` still finds `Bernice Yu`. Searches of one to three characters must match exactly.
* Text after a prefix continues until the next prefix. So `find n/Alex example` searches names for `Alex example`. To search every detail for `example`, put it first: `find example n/Alex`.
* Each `t/` must match one of the contact's tags. If `n/`, `p/`, `e/` or `a/` is repeated, only the last one is used.
* `find` on its own shows no contacts. An empty prefix, such as `n/`, does not narrow the search, except that an empty `t/` shows only contacts with at least one tag.
* Archived contacts are included in the results.
* `find oak` finds contacts with `oak` in any detail, such as the name `Prof Oak` or the address `Oak Street`.
* `find n/Al` finds contacts whose names contain `Al`, such as `Alex Yeoh` and `Roy Balakrishnan`.
* `find example n/Al t/fri` finds contacts with `example` in any detail, `Al` in their name and `fri` in one of their tags.

* `find t/fri t/col` finds contacts with a tag containing `fri` **and** a tag containing `col`, such as Bernice Yu, who is tagged `friends` and `colleagues`. Contacts with only one of these tags are not shown.
![Results for 'find t/fri t/col', requiring both tag conditions to match](images/findTagsFriCol.png)
Shows contacts that have all the given tags. Unlike `find`, which matches part of a tag, `filter` matches only complete tags.
* A contact must have **every** given tag. It may also have other tags.
* Tags must match completely: `filter t/policy` does not match `housing policy`. Use `find t/policy` to match part of a tag.
* Upper/lower case does not matter, so `t/EXPERT` matches `expert`.
* Nothing may come before the first `t/`, and other prefixes such as `n/` are not allowed.
* If any tag is invalid (see [Contact details](#contact-details)), the whole command fails and the list does not change.
* `filter` searches all your contacts, including archived ones, not just the ones shown. It replaces the result of any earlier `find` or `filter`.
* Filtering only changes which contacts are shown. Use `list` to go back to your active contacts.
If no contact matches, ByLine lists every tag in use, so you can pick the exact one:
Available tags: economics, expert, housing policy
* `filter t/housing policy` shows contacts tagged `housing policy`.
* `filter t/housing policy t/expert` shows only contacts with both tags.
* `filter t/housing` does not show contacts tagged only `housing policy`, because the tag must match completely.
Sorts the contacts currently shown by one of their details. Only the order on screen changes; your contacts are not changed.
* `ORDER` is `asc` (A to Z, smallest first) or `desc`. If you leave it out, `asc` is used.
* Upper/lower case does not matter, so `sort NAME DESC` works.
* Names, emails and addresses are sorted alphabetically, ignoring upper/lower case. Phone numbers are sorted as numbers, so `000123` and `123` count as equal.
* `sort tag` uses each contact's alphabetically first tag. Contacts without tags always come last.
* Contacts that are equal on the chosen field are sorted by name, A to Z.
* Only the contacts currently shown are sorted, e.g. the results of a `find`. Running `list`, `find`, `filter`, `add` or `edit` afterwards shows the list unsorted again.
On success, ByLine shows, for example, `Sorted contacts by name in descending order.`
![Result of sorting contacts by name in descending order](images/sortNameDescResult.png)

If the field or order is not one of the above, or there are extra words, ByLine shows an error and the order does not change. For example, `sort name upward` shows `Invalid sort order. ORDER must be asc or desc.`
* `sort name` sorts by name, A to Z.
* `sort phone desc` sorts by phone number, largest first.
* `sort tag` sorts by first tag, with untagged contacts last.
Archives a contact you are no longer working with, without deleting it.
* Archives the contact with the given `ID`. See [Contact IDs](#contact-ids).
* An archived contact keeps all its details and its ID. Its card shows `[Archived]` after the name.

* Archived contacts are hidden by `list` and when ByLine starts. Use `list archive` to see only archived contacts, or `list all` to see every contact. `find` still includes archived contacts in its results.
* If archived contacts are not being shown, e.g. after `list`, the contact disappears from the list once it is archived.
* An archived contact can still be edited, tagged or deleted.
* If the contact is already archived, ByLine shows `This person is already archived.`
* `archive 3`, then `list all`, shows every contact. The archived contact is marked `[Archived]`:
![Charlotte Oliveiro marked as archived in the full list](images/archivedContact.png)
Restores an archived contact, so that it is no longer archived.
* Restores the contact with the given `ID`. See [Contact IDs](#contact-ids).
* If the contact is not archived, ByLine shows `This person is not archived.`
* `list archive` shows the archived contacts. If one of them shows `ID: 4`, `restore 4` restores it and it disappears from the archived list. Run `list` to see it among your active contacts.
* IDs are not reset: the next contact you add still gets a new ID.
* `clear` deletes all contacts. Running `undo` straight after brings them all back.
Undoes the last change to your contacts.
* These commands can be undone: `add`, `edit`, `delete`, `clear`, `archive`, `restore`, `tag`, `untag` and `load`.
* Commands that only change what is shown, such as `list`, `find` and `sort`, are not undone. `undo` skips over them to the last change.
* You can undo up to 20 changes in a row. Older changes can no longer be undone.
* `undo` keeps the current view. For example, after a `find`, ByLine still shows only the contacts that match the search.
* The history of changes is cleared when you close ByLine, so changes made before a restart cannot be undone.
* If there is nothing to undo, ByLine shows `There is nothing to undo.`
* `undo` takes no parameters. Extra words, such as `undo 3`, show an error. Run `undo` again to undo more than one change.
Undoing an `add` also takes back the contact's ID, so the next contact you add gets that same ID. This is the only case in which an ID is used again.
* `delete 3` followed by `undo` brings back the contact with ID 3.
* `tag 2 t/expert`, then `tag 2 t/source`, then `undo` twice removes both tags.
Redoes the last change you undid.
* You can redo each change you undid, in order, until you make a new change.

* After an `undo`, making a new change, e.g. with `add` or `edit`, means the undone changes can no longer be redone. Commands that only change what is shown, such as `list` or `find`, do not affect this.
* Redoing an undone `add` brings the contact back with the same ID.
* Like `undo`, `redo` keeps the current view, and its history is cleared when you close ByLine.
* If there is nothing to redo, ByLine shows `There is nothing to redo.`
* `redo` takes no parameters. Extra words, such as `redo 2`, show an error.
* `delete 3`, then `undo`, then `redo` deletes the contact with ID 3 again.
Saves all your contacts, including archived contacts, to a backup file.

ByLine automatically saves data after every command. You do not need to save manually.

ByLine saves your data automatically in a JSON (text) file, `data/addressbook.json`, inside the folder you started ByLine from. If you followed the [Quick start](#quick-start), this is the folder that contains `ByLine.jar`. Advanced users are welcome to update data directly by editing that data file.

Each contact in the file has an `id`, and the file has a `nextPersonId`, which is the ID the next new contact will get. Do not change these. Changing them can make ByLine reuse old IDs, or make the data file invalid, for example if two contacts have the same ID or an ID is above 999999.

If your changes make the data file invalid, ByLine starts with no contacts at the next run. The invalid file remains on disk until you run a command (ByLine saves after every command). Still, we recommend backing up the file before editing it.

Furthermore, certain edits can cause ByLine to behave in unexpected ways (e.g., if a value entered is outside of the acceptable range). Therefore, edit the data file only if you are confident that you can update it correctly.
**Q**: How do I transfer my data to another computer?

**A**: On the old computer, run `export` and copy the backup file to the new computer. Then run `load` with that file there. You can also copy `data/addressbook.json` from your old ByLine folder into the new one.
